utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I'm sorry for the late start. It appears we had either a lost witness or lost Bench. There seems to be confusion. But the witness was being held until we were here, and we were here waiting for the witness. So, having overcome that problem, we are now able to commence. Now, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just deal with an additional problem? And I'm sorry to interrupt the Court proceedings, but it is important to be dealt with at this time. The next witness is Ambassador Kypr. He was a European Commission monitor. He was -- and will give evidence in relation to background of matters in Vukovar and leading up to the Vukovar incident. He was contacted by the Prosecution, both by telephone and by e-mail, asking what documents that he -- the documents that he has. We informed him that we had one copy of what I will call handwritten notes. It relates to Major Sljivancanin, his name, and some other matters. We did ask whether there were any other documents that he had. He informed us that he had his own notebook. We asked to see the notebook, for it to be faxed through to us, and he was reluctant to do that and said that he would bring them to court, or bring it to court. He arrived on Sunday evening. I saw him yesterday for the first time, and it was then apparent to me that there was a document that had -- I think it's approximately 26 pages of handwritten notes in B/C/S, the Czech language, and English. There has been no suggestion whatsoever in previous trials of the existence of this document. And, as I say, we asked for it, but he was reluctant to provide it to us. And there is, quite simply, nothing one can do in a situation like that. I have come to Court today because, quite clearly, my learned friends have now had copies served on them. I don't have translations either; we are in exactly the same situation. I have gone through the contents of the document. They're clearly relevant and they go to central issues that the Court will have to determine. My learned friends and indeed myself would wish the translation of those documents. They relate to evidence in chief and undoubtedly many matters for cross-examination. I anticipate that it will take two days for that document to be translated. The reason is perfectly straightforward: They're done in code, as well as ordinary English, or ordinary language, whether it be Czech or B/C/S, and it will be necessary for the ambassador to sit down and go through the documents so that there is an accurate translation. As a consequence of that, my learned friends, and they will be more than able to submit on behalf of themselves, will not be in a position to cross-examine until they've got the translations and have had a chance to peruse it. I, for my part, would have thought they would need perhaps no more than one day, but that's a matter for them and their application. Consequently I am not in a position to call any other witness apart from Ambassador Kypr for two reasons: One, I try and ensure that witnesses come at an appropriate time so we don't have a number of witnesses waiting; and secondly, the other witness is Dr. Schou, who is Danish. He will be -- he is also a European Commission monitor, and the source material for Mr. Kypr is exactly the same as for Dr. Schou, and clearly they are interrelated. Your Honour may remember there was an attempt for us to call them earlier, because of the sequence, as much as anything else. Dr. Schou has had medical problems and was not available until after, I think, the 16th of March was the first available date. So the situation as we now have it, is, I regret to say, we're not able to proceed with the next witness, because of the problems that we have with his own unique document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When is it that you would be able to commence leading evidence from the next witness, in your expectation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have gone through the document with him. I haven't been able to take any notes. I've just tried to understand the general structure and the importance of the issues. I would anticipate that if he sits down with a language assistant or a translator that it would take approximately a day for the original document to be transformed into intelligible -- an intelligible format in B/C/S, and obviously from the Czech language into English and B/C/S, but equally the English has to be translated into B/C/S also. It's handwritten, and with the most respect to him, his handwriting is not always the clearest. So I would have thought a one day for the translation to be done, one day for it to be ensured that it is accurate, it would be served, I hope, then on Thursday morning. That is the timetable, the best case scenario that I can think of. So it would not be ready, I would have thought, at the earliest, before Thursday morning. So we would lose a day, maybe two or three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What length of time do you anticipate that the witness will take?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will be taking the witness in chief. I would anticipate that will take five hours, something like that. I would consider that the length of time would be about the same as Colonel Vujic, perhaps slightly less, but there are various areas that one goes into, and it's sometimes rather difficult to assess how long that's going to take. It deals with other areas as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: From what you say, the practical question boils down to whether the witness should commence on Friday this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. For my part, I am quite prepared to start on Friday. I have no difficulty. I think the difficulty will be whether my learned friends will have enough time to cross-examine. But, having said that, I can certainly take in chief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I am assuming that they would not cross-examine until next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's what I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you intend to take five hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If I took the witness in chief on Friday, then clearly my learned friends would have some time, I would have thought, to prepare cross-examination, to start cross-examination on Monday. I apologise for the delay, but it's not of my making, neither is it of the defence making. It's just, I'm afraid, one of those things that happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Start on Thursday would seem at the moment to be unreasonable. A, we can't be confident hat the document will be ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: B, if it is ready, Defence counsel would not have had an opportunity to study it, so that they would be at a disadvantage as the evidence in chief was given. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The position seems to be that we must adjourn at the end of the evidence of the present witness to resume on Friday morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Does Your Honour want to see the e-mails that were sent to the ambassador, or does Your Honour accept my word?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have what counsel has indicated to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone else. Just a few words on behalf of the Defence. My friends and I consulted each other visually only, and we think that we can start next week with the cross-examination of this witness, providing that we receive the translation simultaneously with the Prosecution, so that we can go over it with our clients. What concerns us and what we need to bring to your attention, is that this document seems to be very important, and it seems to resemble, in its form, the diary of Ambassador Okun. There will be a lot of documents discussed as part of it. Part of this document was available to the Prosecution back in 1996; certainly within the Dokmanovic trial. One page of that diary was already subject of evidence of a witness. What surprises us is that this document, which was placed on the first 65 ter list, was not given to us earlier, and now we have only three or four days to analyse this document. We are, therefore, kindly asking the Chamber this: Should we find something in this document that requires further examination on our part, then we would like to be given an opportunity later to complete the cross-examination. We would prefer not to take this course of action, but right now we don't know, because we don't know what is contained in this document, and this is why we want to inform you of this reservation that we have concerning the document. Otherwise we are quite prepared to commence with our work and to start analysing the document with our clients. I need to make a correction. In relation to the transcript, it's not that the document was on the first 65 ter list; it's that the name of this witness was put on the first 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. The Chamber sees little point at the moment in going over issues as to why this occurred. Our concern is to ensure that, it having occurred, the trial can continue with fairness and as quickly as possible. We will start the evidence of the witness on Friday. Should there be some basis for concern, it can be raised by Defence counsel, either on Friday or when they commence cross-examination, and it will be assessed on its merit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just say, we did not have the document. We have -- on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, you've explained it. We understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you indeed. There being no other matters, we might continue with the evidence. May I remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, have you completed entirely?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have completed my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Karlovic. My name is Vladimir Domazet. I am one of the Defence counsel of Mr. Mrksic, and I will be putting some questions to you regarding your examination-in-chief. Given that both of us speak the same language, in order to ensure the accuracy of the transcript, I will ask you something that I will try to observe myself, which is to always make pauses between questions and answers so that what we say can be translated into English and recorded properly. First of all, Mr. Karlovic, something very brief concerning your personal information. Yesterday in examination-in-chief I think that you said to my learned friend that you are an owner of a building company, or something similar. It is not the most relevant issue, but six months ago when you testified in Belgrade you described yourself as a retiree, as a pensioner. So which of the two is correct? Or have there been any changes in your status?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both of those things are correct. I am retired, and I am also an owner of a building construction company.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You have retired as an officer of the Croatian army; is that correct? Up until 2002 you were a member of the Croatian army, which means that you were eligible for retirement based on your service with the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became eligible for retirement based on my health condition and disabilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. But in addition to serving in the army, you didn't have any other years of service that contributed to your being able to retire?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yesterday in examination-in-chief you said that you didn't serve in the JNA and that the first army where you served was the Croatian army, which you joined in August of 1991. My question is this: You completed your high school, or the secondary school in 1989, and based on the then existing laws in the country, you were supposed to go and serve in the army immediately after completing secondary education. How come you didn't go to the army at that point? Were you exempted? Did you go through the recruitment process and all other procedures that accompany? Did you complete that in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I graduated from secondary school in 1989; you are correct. It was in 1989. I married in 1990. And since my wife was 16 and a half at the time when we got married, I asked for postponement of my military service so that I could support my wife and the child that was on its way. I don't know whether I answered all parts of your question. If I haven't, would you please refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, you have. You have answered. The only other follow-up question I have is that: Does this mean you were granted a postponement in relation to your military service and that this is why you didn't go into the army until later on, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was given an official legal postponement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You said yesterday, and you also stated this in your statements, that in August of 1991 you joined the Croatian army and that you had a 15- to 20-day training in Kumrovec; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I can't vouch that it's fully accurate in terms of the days, but something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Regardless of whether it was 15- or 20-day training, will you agree with me that it's rather a short time for military training, for a proper military training? So would you please explain to me what kind of training did you receive in that brief period of time? What kind of soldier training?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite correct. That is definitely too short a period for a proper military training. There was hardly enough time to teach us anything else but the basics of infantry training, how to shoot and so on, that was an abbreviated form of training.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Within that training did you have any instruction in terms of the rights and duties of soldiers? As you have said yourself, it was clear that a conflict was in the making. Therefore, tell me: Did somebody tell you what would be your rights and duties if you were to capture an enemy soldier, or vice versa, if you yourself were captured?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we naturally had that type of training too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you told in the training, or did you perhaps know at the time, something about the JNA ranks?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. As an explanation for going into the Croatian army on a voluntary basis, you said that you wanted to defend the homeland, if I'm not mistaken. You said that at the time Croatia had been attacked and when asked by my learned friend by whom, you said by the JNA. And then you added yourself that the most critical parts were Eastern Slavonia, Lika, southern part, and Banija. Do you remember giving this reply?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I would like to know what you meant when you said, "Southern part," because other geographical regions are quite clear?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to a portion of Dalmatia, to the southern portion. Sibenik region, Zadar region, if that is indeed in the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you also refer to the area around Knin when you said that or not?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll be quite frank, I didn't even consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned these four regions as being critical in your view at the time. Can we agree that these regions were precisely the areas containing a significant percentage of Serbian population, and in some areas Serbs were the dominant population?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can agree on that. And we can also agree that a significant portion of Croatian population also lived in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. Karlovic, because we are talking about Croatia. However, these regions were populated by a significant amount of Serbs, and this is probably why you termed them critical areas, and this is probably what contributed to the eruption of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that. I cannot agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You cannot agree with me in saying that tensions erupted or escalated?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't agree in that portion of your sentence. There were no tensions among the population because the population does not have tanks, weaponry and so on. The population never goes into war. The residents don't have any mortars at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. This is your view. I will not dwell on this topic. It will be up to others to analyse it.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I would now like to turn to something else. You mentioned several places that you visited before your unit came to Vukovar. I, for my part, am interested only in Vukovar. You said that during the night between the 30th September and the 1st October you arrived in Vukovar via Bogdanovci and Luzac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You explained that you reached Bogdanovci by bus and then walked via Luzac to Vukovar. That night did you have any kind of a conflict with the JNA, or were you able to reach Vukovar without any conflict?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were too small a group in order to be able to engage in any sort of conflict. Had there been any conflict, we would not have been able to reach Vukovar. This must be clear to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, naturally. Based on your answer, I can conclude that there were only 21 soldiers in your group. There was no larger unit arriving there simultaneously. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You also said that you relieved another unit there; I suppose another unit from your brigade which either left Vukovar or remained there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left Vukovar that same night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And I suppose they used the same route to leave Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I can only guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Karlovic, you said that this unit was under the command of Tihomir Perkovic, and that Josip Nemec was his deputy, they were senior officers. What were their ranks, did they hold any ranks at the time and what was their military background or training?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for ranks, we did not have any ranks at the time. We only had posts. As for their military education, I really know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your unit numbering 21 soldiers, I assume this number included the two of them as well. Were you some kind of a special unit or was this just what you said, a unit that belonged to the 1st Brigade, I think?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were part of the National Guards Corps, members of the 1st Brigade. We were not known as a special unit or anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, you said 1st Brigade, 4th Battalion, 3rd Company. Were you part of the 3rd Company or were you the 3rd Company?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were the 3rd Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Karlovic, do you know where the headquarters of the brigade or battalion was and who was in charge of the brigade or the battalion?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm thinking about the commander. And, to tell you the truth, I really don't know who was the commander of the brigade. I can give you two names. One of them most likely was the commander. I think that Mr. Rukavina, General Rukavina and General Josip Lucic were in charge. I don't know where the headquarters was. I can also give you a probable location where the headquarters was, but I'm not fully certain. I think that the headquarters of the brigade was in Rakitje, in the vicinity of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. The names that you gave us as the possible names of the commanders, these people were not in Vukovar at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I never saw them in Vukovar. And at the time, in fact, I didn't even known these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Speaking about your unit, you said that -- you mentioned something about weapons, personal weapons, about rifles, automatic rifles. This is what you mentioned in your statement. My question is: Did you have launchers, hand-held launchers?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had so-called Zoljas. These are disposable rocket launchers. The gentlemen will know what I'm talking about. And I said that each one of us was also issued two hand-grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You had that along with your personal weapons, automatic rifles; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that you had a uniform; you even explained the insignia that you had on the uniform. What I'm interested is one detail that appeared later, you will remember when, and that was that you had yellow boots on. That footwear, was that issued to you in Vukovar itself or did you come to Vukovar with the footwear?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was issued in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: During your stay in Vukovar, since you changed positions while you were in Vukovar, do you know that besides the local population that took part in the defence of Vukovar, do you know if there were any other units; for example, any other soldiers or members of the police who took part in the defence?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the HOS units? If not, maybe we can clarify that. You know what HOS was at the time, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that there were HOS units in Vukovar, but I was never in any kind of contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did your unit have its headquarters, or was it under the command of some other headquarters in Vukovar itself? And if that was so, where was the command?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't have any sort of headquarters of command -- or command of our own. We were subordinated to the command of the town defence. Once I was sitting in a truck while we were waiting in front of this bunker where the town defence command was located. I was never inside, though. I know who was in command, though. Is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. For the purposes of the transcript, yes. Please tell us who was in command and where was this -- these headquarters where you were at one time?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time the commander was Mr. Dedakovic, and I know that it was located in the centre of town. I don't know exactly where, though. I don't know the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Karlovic, do you know where the Eltz castle was? Do you ever go there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was never at the Eltz castle, so I don't remember where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you ever hear what was located there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just to check on some things that you mentioned yesterday, when you talked about artillery fire at your positions, first of all, you said that you were able to confirm the direction of fire when the shooting was coming from the direction of Vojvodina, from across the Danube, whereas the other fire you could not determine where it was coming from because it was being fired from different directions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You also talked about occasional fly-overs and air force attacks by the JNA. Do you know if, at the time when you were there or in the previous period, there were any planes knocked down over Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I mentioned planes or not, but what you say is correct, there were fly-overs. As for planes being brought down, I never saw anything like that myself, but I did hear that planes were downed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember whether these planes that were down, which period was that in, was it before you arrived at Vukovar, or when you were already there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your first position was at the silo. You explained that -- where the silo was, and you explained the significance of it. Your unit, or some other unit, did it actually use the silo, did you climb on top of it or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we used it. I mean we were billeted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you were the commander of a squad or actually of a half of that unit; is that correct? So following these other two men that you mentioned, you were also some kind of commander of a half of the unit of this squad of men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: One more question on this topic. It was about how you were supplied for the time that you were there. Where did you get your food from? Do you know whether the food was distributed from some central location?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that the truck brought food every day, but I don't know where it came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday in response to a question by my learned friend about the differences between the JNA, different formations, soldiers, you provided a detailed explanation. So I don't have any particular questions except regarding one point, which I would like to clarify. You said that the reserve forces were part of the regular JNA forces. By that were you thinking of those reservists who were mobilised in the regular procedure and joined the JNA units, or were you thinking generally of reservists who existed and, according to regulations, had been issued with uniforms which they kept at home in expectation of being called up? So are you talking about regularly mobilised reservists, or reservists who reported without actually being called up, who did it voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yesterday I didn't really differentiate between these two groups, but I did tell you now that I believe that both of these kinds of reservists were members of the JNA. As far as I'm concerned, the two are the same. The description of the uniforms that I provided, and I told the Prosecutor that, that is my judgement, that is how I saw these particulars. I apologise if I'm going too fast for the court reporter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I agree with you that a reservist who is summoned would then come and join the unit and becomes a part of that army regardless of the young soldiers, the conscripts who were there serving in the regular -- their regular term of duty. But what about these others who were reservists without having been called up who participated in combat? In your opinion, could they also be considered reservists without officially be called up to join the units?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you will agree with me that I am not able to know who actually received a summons and who didn't. I looked at the soldiers and I sorted them out according to which possible group they could belong to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Perhaps in this particular way we are not able to understand each other. I did want to make a difference between these two groups, even though you explained when I say that these others, or the Territorial Defence members wore different uniforms, so they could be clearly differentiated from the regular JNA soldiers. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could tell the difference between them, but I don't know if I was right or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When we're talking about the combat in Vukovar, you mentioned that after 20 days or so you pulled back from the line at the silo and you went to the Prvomajska Street where you participated in the fighting and gradually withdrew towards the centre as the operations proceeded; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So in that period you probably did participate in combat, direct combat, compared to the period spent at the silo where you said there was no direct combat. So in that period did you see your unit, or maybe some other unit, with captured JNA soldiers or wounded JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have the opportunity to see any captured soldiers belonging to the JNA or any other group. I don't recollect my group ever being in such a situation. However, we were in a different position when we came to those positions. We were no longer one group only. We had been broken up and distributed or allocated to different groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I understand. So this 21-man unit was broken up and deployed to different units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were at different positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I understood from your answers that you knew where the police station in Vukovar was?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you go to that police station when it was still functioning as a police station?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear that there was a prison in the police station that had been turned into a prison for prisoners of war, or for those who were captured?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In mid-November, you were explaining actually the situation in Vukovar in mid-November, and it was your assessment, and not only yours, that it was only a matter of days before Vukovar fell. You personally were trying to work out what you were going to do, and you also described what you were doing over those last few days, the period that you came to the hospital. Was your unit all together at that time, and were you trying to see at the level of your unit as a whole headed by your commander, Perkovic, what you were going to do, whether you were going to try to make a break-through or remain in Vukovar as a unit?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were no longer a unit as a whole. Our commander, Perkovic, left Vukovar that same evening, so it's like I'm making a kind of digression. As far as the agony of the fall of the town, you could already see on the 1st of November that it was only a question of time before the town fell. This did not become apparent, only later towards the middle of the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that you mentioned your commander, Perkovic, and that he left, I didn't understand exactly when was it that he left?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same night that we arrived at Vukovar was the night that he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Are you thinking of the 1st of October when you just arrived? He didn't stay with you that whole time?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. In October. And he didn't stay with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So who was commanding your unit, if he wasn't with you that whole time?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Josip Nemec.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said yesterday, as well as in previous statements, that you decided to go to the hospital and surrender there, because you were expecting that the JNA would enter Vukovar and the hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At the end of his examination my learned friend went through all of the statements you provided in different proceedings. And one by one you confirmed that all the statements he mentioned yesterday were yours, that you remembered them, and of course you said that you always spoke the truth and nothing but the truth in those statements. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I would like to ask you something about your 1995 statement to investigators from the OTP in relation to the hospital. I think perhaps that -- well, you probably don't have the statement in front of you, so it would be good for me to provide you with a copy of this statement, so that you could confirm whether what I read out is actually stated in the statement.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you go ahead and read it out. I -- I trust you. I believe what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, I would still prefer if you had a copy. So could the usher please give you a copy and then ... Please, if you would look at page 3, paragraph 3; and for my learned friends, the English version is also on page 3, but it's paragraph 5. When you said that those who wanted to -- to could take off their uniforms and put on civilian clothing. "When I arrived at the hospital with all the others, we were told to take off the uniforms and put on civilian clothing using whatever clothes they could find." Did you find that?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is that what it says in your statement?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I can just say, you didn't read it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, then you read it correctly.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "When I arrived at the hospital, all of the other soldiers were told." This is very different from what you said. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I ask you, Mr. Karlovic, to go back to the habit of watching the screen and waiting for the last question to finish on the screen before you answer? If you can try and remember that. And, Mr. Domazet, if could you try the same. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. So in order to avoid any confusion we will read it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So it says in the statement: "When I arrived at the hospital, all of the other soldiers were told to take off their uniforms and put on civilian clothing using whatever clothes they could find." You confirmed that that is part of your statement. I'm asking you: Who was it who told these soldiers to do this?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I known who it was who said it, then I would have said that at the time. What I said was that this was stated, but I don't know who said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. So you don't know who said this, that's fine. You spent at least three days and three nights in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I think that you said that during that time your names were not taken down, no list was created. My question is: Throughout that period of time, did anybody from the hospital or from anywhere else ask you what you were doing there, you and the others? How was it possible for you to stay so long there without anybody asking you anything? Because you, for example, were not wounded, and you were not named as a patient, were you?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I didn't quite understand your question. You are asking me how come nobody asked me anything ever. I don't know how to answer. I don't know how come nobody ever asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you are confirming that throughout that time nobody ever asked you what you were doing there, how come you were there, you were not put on any list?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned seeing the first JNA members on the 19th. You said that there were no problems and that their attitude was such that they were quite friendly, peaceful; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It was on the 19th. On the 20th, you described us the situation when you were lined up, searched, in order to find any weapons, and then you were sent to buses. You didn't say anything about this, but I suppose that no weapons were found on anyone; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. As far as I remember, no weapons were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, that whole procedure of searching and entering buses, you described as properly conducted; is that right? You had no complaints about the treatment you received from soldiers.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was normal military conduct. At the time there were no outbursts, no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said in the barracks in your bus there were two soldiers. I suppose two soldiers in addition to the driver who did not allow anyone to get on the bus, even though the people outside were pressuring them to enter the bus, the people outside who were insulting people. So I suppose that you viewed this conduct of the JNA soldiers as a proper one?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a proper one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you left the barracks and came to Ovcara, you encountered there a totally different scene. You described to us how you left the buses and then you said that you saw JNA soldiers there as well. So I suppose that these were the soldiers who were already there when the buses arrived. That was your conclusion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let's leave aside those whom you identified as Chetniks, members of TO and the others. Let us now focus on the soldiers who stood around the hangar, those that you saw. Can you tell me what kind of uniforms they had? You identified both olive-drab and camouflage uniforms, so which type did they have?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they had both. I can't tell you which ones were more numerous. You will understand that it's been 15 years, so quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember what they had on their heads, was it helmets, caps?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some had helmets, some had caps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were you able to see who was in command of these JNA soldiers, did they have somebody who commanded over them while you were there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I saw or was able to identify who was his commander individually. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. But you mentioned some officers, you mentioned a colonel whose last name you weren't sure of. Let me remind you, you mentioned several possible last names for this colonel, Ivankovic, Ivanovic, something like that. You also mentioned a person with the last name Ivankovic who was the son of Dr. Ivankovic. So when talking of this colonel, I suppose you did not have in mind the son of Dr. Ivankovic?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So this is a different person, an entirely different officer of the JNA. My question is this: Was it perhaps Colonel Vojinovic? Would this assist you in remembering? Is it possible that this colonel's last name was Vojinovic?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, it would be ridiculous and improper for me to accept Vojinovic as the actual last name. The last names that I gave you were the ones that stuck in my head, and Vojinovic means nothing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, it's been a long time. You gave three or four possible last names for this colonel. I was just trying to see whether it was possible that it was this man.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish I knew the last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it was only two names that the witness offered, Mr. Domazet, not three or four.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that in the statement I saw a third last name, Jovanovic. But at any rate we now clarified that it was not Vojinovic. The witness gave us his answer, and I thank him for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What I would like to know is who set up the gauntlet, the gauntlet through which people entering the hangar had to go and were beaten as they went through it. When answering the questions of my learned friend yesterday, I think that you said that everybody joined this gauntlet, and if "everybody" includes the JNA soldiers, then I would like to know that. Therefore, did the JNA soldiers join the gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody took part in the beating, both in front of the hangar and inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. Let's separate what happened in the hangar and what happened outside, and especially in the gauntlet. I'm asking you now about what took place outside. In the gauntlet you said that the two lines were formed, two columns of people, a so-called gauntlet. Do you remember regular JNA soldiers being in that gauntlet? Did they beat you as well?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And if I may expand. The JNA soldiers came to the gauntlet to take groups of people and usher them inside the hangar. So it was hard to see, discern exactly what was going on. There were JNA soldiers in the gauntlet, but the majority of those in the gauntlet were Chetniks and TO men. I hope I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is that what you said in your prior statements?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't go into details. I don't remember anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you please take the statement in front of you. This is your 1995 statement, page 4. I think passage 10, paragraph 10, which begins with the words: "The buses were lined up." In English, that's page 5, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm interested only in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm saying this for the benefit of the Prosecutor. I will read this out and you will tell me whether that's correct. "The buses were lined up, one behind the other. The first bus was level with the entrance to the hangar. We were all made to get out of the buses and when I got out I saw that there were two lines of Chetniks standing on either side of the entrance to the hangar. Everyone was forced to walk in between the lines of Chetniks, and while I was standing in line, I saw that people were being beaten by the Chetniks as they went through the lines, beaten with wooden poles, chains, and gun-butts. People were also having their clothes taken off them, which resulted in some of the men ending up wearing only their underwear." Is that correct what I read out?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you see that in three places in this paragraph you say that it was only Chetniks who made up the gauntlet, that it was only them who beat the people, and no TO men are mentioned and no soldiers are mentioned. This is the statement that you gave back in 1995, and you never varied it until yesterday when you gave a somewhat different description, including the JNA soldiers in the gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say in the statement that it was only the Chetniks who beat the people. And I continue to affirm that those who beat the people were mostly Chetniks. It was mostly them who made up the gauntlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But you will agree with me that you didn't state so in your statement? In your statement you mentioned only Chetniks. You never mentioned who made the majority or not. You mentioned exclusively Chetniks in your statement. You spoke about the beating inside the hangar. Yesterday, as well as in your prior statements, you said that you stayed in the hangar for a very brief time. You estimated that it was three to four minutes. You said that you were hit several times, you received several blows, but then somebody came with a captain and then you described that the beating stopped and you were taken outside. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can we agree that during that brief period of time while you were in the hangar and when you were beaten, you did not have sufficient time to observe what was going on in the rest of the hangar, to see who beat whom, and who did the beating, members of which groups? So that's what I'm interested now. To what extent were you able to observe what was going on in the hangar, considering that you were there just a very brief period of time, and you were beaten yourself?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, three to four minutes isn't all that brief. That's the first thing I wanted to say. The second thing is, upon entering the hangar, one can observe the entire scene. So you can definitely see what's going on. 10 seconds is a brief period of time. Three to four minutes is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Approximately six months ago you testified in Belgrade in front of the court there. We have a transcript of the trial in Belgrade, and every word is recorded in it, just like here. I would like to give you this transcript now so that you can confirm to us whether you indeed stated this in Belgrade. Could the usher please assist us?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's important to add is that in the Belgrade trial I was defence witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said in that trial that you were testifying for defence, and if you remember, the president of the trial chamber told you that they did not discern between prosecution and defence witnesses, that the witnesses were there to tell the truth. And when you say that you testified for the defence, you probably meant those two accused that you mentioned yesterday?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that those two accused were accused as members of paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know what capacity they had. Whether they were members of paramilitary formations, reserve forces, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you please look at page 20 of the transcript? Can you find the part of your answer where you testified precisely on this topic and then you say: "I didn't look very carefully to see who hit whom, but one could hear that people had to put their heads down and keep their hands on their shoulders." Were you able to find this?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 20. 20/45; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it at the top of the page, the middle of the page, the bottom of the page? I can't ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, I wasn't really looking that specifically who was hitting who, but you could hear that people had to keep their heads down and their hands behind their backs. I received a few blows. And then you say: "I wasn't there for long, three for four minutes." And this is not in dispute. So even for yourself, as far as you're concerned, you say that you don't know who beat you, you say you didn't really watch, that it didn't take that long. So you still abide by the statement that there were JNA soldiers who took part in that.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that I didn't really pay that much attention, and I stand by what I said, that everybody took part in the beating. But I wasn't really looking at how many people beat how many other people, whether all of them were beating everybody or some were beating some people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, this is also about your estimate of the numbers. Yesterday you told my learned friend about how many soldiers there were, you gave your estimate of the number of soldiers in the hangar, as well as outside of it. Do you remember that in Belgrade you were also asked about this. Even the president of the trial chamber insisted, and you kept saying that after such a long time you really couldn't recall the number. Could you please look at page 13. It's page 13, line 8 or 9, that begins -- I'm going to read and you can follow. The president of the trial chamber asks: "How many, in your estimates, were there in the Chetnik formations and those belonging to the JNA?" Your answer: "Please don't take it badly, but I cannot remember." The president of the trial chamber: "Some estimates, you cannot give us anything like that?" Your answer: "I dare not make any estimates. It would be absolutely improper after 14 years for me to give an estimate. I don't know." Did I read correctly what is stated here?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you notice that then you did not want to give the number in answer to the president's question, and you said that after so many years you didn't want to state anything which you were not sure about, but yesterday you did give an estimate?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I absolutely agree with you. First of all, yes, when I testified in Belgrade at that time I didn't know what I would be asked and I wasn't prepared for any sort of estimates, and the estimates I did give were just my views about the numbers and they don't have to be correct. So I more or less knew what I would be asked, I had time to think about it, and I gave figures to the prosecutors and I also told them that they need necessarily not be correct. So I absolutely agree with you. What you say is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understand you correctly, your estimate of yesterday is your estimate, it need not necessarily be correct, because so much time has passed since then?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we're talking about my estimates. That's what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am completing this topic, and I don't have too much to go, but I think that still this is a good moment for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. It's just about time for the tapes to change. We will resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karlovic, before we move on to a different topic, I wanted to ask you the last -- one last thing about Ovcara. As concerns the gauntlet, I wanted to show you what you stated during the Dokmanovic case. This is an excerpt from the transcript in English. I am about to read it aloud, and my colleague will follow whether I am reading correctly. And you also said that the Chetniks formed the gauntlet and you didn't mention anyone else. This is page 751 in the Dokmanovic case: "[In English] When you personally had to get off the bus?" [Interpretation] Your reply: "[In English] I saw that in front of the hangar a gauntlet or -- was -- was created by the Chetniks, and people were passing through there." [Interpretation] Therefore, during the Dokmanovic case you stated somewhat similar to what you said in Belgrade, and yet here yesterday and today you spoke about soldiers participating for the first time. I believe you still abide by the explanation given before?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said a while ago, it was the Chetniks who made up the gauntlet, but it was not able for the other soldiers not to participate. Hence, I don't see your point clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Karlovic, to move on to what happened at Velepromet and Modateks, and I have a few questions in relation to that. I believe you said that you were escorted to Modateks by the person who introduced himself to you as Stuka?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And I believe you said that he returned to Ovcara. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I remember. There were several of them. There were four of them, and they were talking about the fact that they were supposed to go back, that they had to go back. I felt unsafe without them, I asked them if they could stay with us. And he said that he was supposed to go back. That's why I said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But as to whether they returned indeed, you don't know that, because you never saw them again?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As for the remaining six out of your group of seven who came to Modateks, all six of them were together with you tomorrow [as interpreted] in Modateks and Velepromet as well?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned a person who was in charge in Modateks, and his nickname was Deda. Did he hold any rank, was he a military person or --

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't know for sure, but I can offer my opinion. As for his rank, I didn't know whether he held any, but I know he was an elderly man.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know whether he held any rank at all, whether he belonged to the military?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he had any rank, but he was superior to those soldiers who were there with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As for the other person at Velepromet for whom you said he commanded over the military policemen, you also told him that he -- told that I didn't have a white belt, hence you couldn't identify him as a military policeman. Why do you believe he was the commander there and what was his uniform like, since you said he had no white belt?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you understood what I said yesterday as to who it was that didn't have a white belt. I didn't have in mind the person who commanded at Velepromet, but about a person who was together with the military policemen that escorted me to Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you explain further, please? I probably misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who commanded at Velepromet did bear the military police insignia, and as far as I can remember, I believe he had a white belt. I don't know whether he had any belt supports across his shoulder. I don't think I ever mentioned his white belt ever, but this is the person whom I thought was the commander of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned the person from whom you later found out was the commander of the barracks in Vukovar, and you said that he took you to the barracks in his own private vehicle of Opel make?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As is stated in the transcript in the Ovcara case, and I can remind you, I believe you didn't mention that yesterday, but he supposedly said that when he was talking to the commander you mentioned that you said they were cursing, and you said he mentioned something along the lines that, "We have dealt with the Ustashas and it seems now that we will have to deal with the Chetniks."

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I spoke about that yesterday, it didn't seem to be important enough to mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But in your assessment, he was the barracks commander and had he stated something along those lines at the time?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: He took you to the barracks in his own vehicle, the rest went by bus. And as far as I understood, they treated you fairly in the barracks. I believe you were given food and water, and I think you said that they were correct in their communication with you during that night?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you discussed Mitrovica where you spent some six months, you said that you were interrogated on several occasions, but that you were never treated as a suspect and that no proceedings were ever initiated against you. Did you know that there were proceedings instituted against some other people held at Mitrovica; for example, some were charged with armed rebellion and some of them even faced a court and they were sentenced afterwards?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But you were in the charged with anything, that in particular?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: During the interrogations, did you speak about your role in Vukovar and about the events you participated in, or did you try to avoid the topic?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent I was able to avoid it, I didn't mention those things. I never hid, though, that I was a soldier, that I was a part of the 1st Brigade, and I told them what battalion I belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I believe you said yesterday that several people participated in the interrogations, and that you couldn't remember their names. I wanted to put a name to you or, rather, whether any of those people who interrogated you ever introduced themselves as Colonel Branko?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: During the interrogations, did they ever ask you about Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And you didn't discuss it with anyone yourself, did you?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you mentioned the Belgrade proceedings, and as you stated today, you said that you believed to be a defence witness there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you have in mind the defence of the two people you knew at the time under their nicknames of Kinez and Mare?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that it was during the proceedings in Belgrade you learned of their real and full names?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are partially correct, and if I may explain, I will do so. As concerns Predrag Milojevic, I heard of him before as being someone referred to as Kinez, but I didn't know he was that person at the time, because I believe he was wanted for war crimes in Croatia. I read that in the Croatian press. At that time I couldn't believe it was the same person. I had heard of Kinez before, but in Belgrade I just realised that indeed it was the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The incident you testified about, and you tried to explain to the Belgrade court how those two people treated you and that it should be taken into account, am I right if I say that concerning the incident you never stated anything or you never spoke about it with anyone in 1995, in 1996, or in 1998 in the Dokmanovic case, and that for the first time in December 2005 was the first time you discussed that incident and the Velepromet incident?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to expand on -- in my explanation. As regards my discussion with the investigators of the OTP, the entire story always ended with Ovcara. We never got as far as Velepromet. In Croatia, though, I gave a detailed account to the security service that lasted for two days, and I mentioned there Kinez and Mare, clearly. And the OTP asked me about what happened after -- afterwards only later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That is your explanation. But am I correct in saying that it was indeed the first time you mentioned that and that it appeared in the statement, because in your statement of 1995, and in the Dokmanovic case, it never appeared? You never mentioned Velepromet and the incident in relation to the two people.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to provide a statement as regards Velepromet, but the investigator was not interested in the sequence of events afterwards. Hence, it was for the first time in Belgrade that I gave an official statement concerning Velepromet to anyone, be it investigators or a court. And this is the first time I spoke about the two people who saved me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That's precisely what I said. It was the first time you officially spoke about what happened at Velepromet and in that house after you were rescued by the two people?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we disregard my statement to the Croatian Security Service, yes, then before the Belgrade tribunal, that was the first time I mentioned officially Kinez and Mare.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: A minute ago you said that you didn't know whether the Belgrade trial considered the group paramilitary or anything else, but you, I believe, were able to make your own conclusions as to whether there were any active JNA officers amongst the group or whether there were what you called members of the TO or Chetniks or something else, as regards the people who were tried in Belgrade, if you can answer that.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: A minute ago, replying to one of my questions, you said that you didn't know whether they belonged to the paramilitaries, as regards the two people that you testified in favour of. But I'm asking about the entire group, whether you know whether there were any JNA officers among the group or whether those were exclusively people from some other, be it paramilitary or Chetnik or TO, formations?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who they belonged to. I wasn't interested in the Belgrade trial up until the moment when I was supposed to appear there as a witness for those two people, if my answer suffices.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I believe you reiterated what I stated in my question, and that is that during a hearing in Belgrade -- I will put this question yet again. Your comment, as regards the Belgrade trial, and I believe you still abide by it, that luckily Ljuboja was acquitted but unfortunately Kinez received a maximum sentence of 20 years?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I stick to that opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The differences between your statement and your testimony yesterday and today as regards the role of certain JNA soldiers, does it have anything to do with the Belgrade proceedings? Because other people were tried there, and here we have JNA officers being tried and that in Belgrade perhaps you tried to minimise the guilt of the people who were charged there, and yet you are trying to increase the responsibility of people being tried here?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe your question to be a very unfair one. Those two people saved my life. I have six children today. I am alive, thanks to them, and that's why I went to Belgrade to testify. I would be very happy if these three people here were proven not guilty, and I do not look at the incidents in regards -- or pertaining to individual people, but I simply see that as being one big tragic situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karlovic, I hope I was being fair in my questions.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Karlovic. I am Borivoje Borovic, attorney-at-law.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Which rank did you have in the Croatian army before you retired?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that you were a Croatian army soldier in 1991. My question is: Was this an organised army in terms of uniforms, weapons, command, and so on?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my point of view, I can say that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Members of the ZNG, were they Croatian army component, or was that special formation or was that part of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to respond to that question. I don't know where National Guards units belonged to, whether they were part of the MUP. I don't know whether the military command had already been set up or not. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you have information that they did not belong to the official Croatian army that you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered that I don't know. I can't say either way, because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you came to Vukovar, were all Croatian army members armed and did they all have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, they all did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see combined units of the ZNG and the Croatian army out in the field? Was that how it was?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You must understand that, as far as I'm concerned, ZNG was the Croatian army at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that we agree that the members of the ZNG, as a part of the Croatian army, were all armed, and if they were armed, what sort of weapons did they have?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that we had infantry weapons and I described the type. We also had rocket launchers and we also had our hand-grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that members of the ZNG in your units had similar types of weapons and were they all issued with such weapons?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can recall, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the course of 1991 Yugoslav army barracks were blockaded? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Who blockaded those barracks, and what do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. I wasn't near any barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the barracks after the blockade were accessible to members of the Croatian forces and members of the JNA were moved out of those barracks? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I really cannot talk about that because --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware of the fact -- or, rather, my question is: Did you know that the Vukovar barracks was also blockaded in the same way that the other barracks in Croatia were blockaded?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I -- I'm not aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that you took part in Flash and Storm operations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: During that operation were not more than 300.000 civilians, Serbs from Croatia, expelled? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not want to respond to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you belonged to the 1st Brigade, 4th Battalion, 3rd Company; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That brigade, was it in Zagreb or Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command was in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about -- and the members of the brigade were in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in different places, not only in Vukovar. But a part were in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of the 204th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what you know about that brigade?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything. I know it's the 204th Brigade and that it's from Vukovar. As for who commanded it or what it did, I -- I really don't know. I know very little about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you arrived at Vukovar, did you see volunteers from other towns there? I think you mentioned that?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were some.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: From which cities?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already mentioned some. Perhaps not all of them, but they were volunteers from Zagreb, Varazdin, Cakovec, Vinkovci, Osijek. All of those places.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were all those volunteers also in uniform and armed?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see all of them, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The ones that you did see though?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were similarly dressed and equipped, as we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You described --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, could we see Exhibit 156 on the screen now, please? I'm going to show you now a map that you already looked at. Could you please zoom in a little bit? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Question for the witness: Could the usher please help you and could you please take the red pen and draw a line indicating the direction from which you arrived at Vukovar, which you moved in and where you ended up?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that from Bogdanovci we came to Luzac. I'm going to draw an arrow. I don't know which roads we used. I know we went through fields, through cornfields, so I really cannot draw the exact route that we took.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But just indicate where you ended up.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Luzac, and then we ended up at the silo, which I already talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please indicate that?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we -- I would like to tender this as an exhibit, Your Honour. And we can indicate Bogdanovci with the letter A, and your -- the point where you ended up, or your destination, could we mark that with the letter B?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Your Honours, could we please have this tendered as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 296.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Next question: Did you go from point A to point B without any armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've already said that. That's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
